content: Aeromonas is a gram-negative, facultative anaerobic rod-shaped bacterium that morphologically resembles members of the Enterobacteriaceae family. Fourteen species of Aeromonas have been identified, most of which are associated with human diseases. The most clinically significant pathogens within this genus are Aeromonas hydrophila, Aeromonas caviae, and Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria. These organisms are widely distributed in freshwater and brackish water environments. Aeromonas is primarily associated with two major types of diseases: gastroenteritis and wound infections, which may or may not be accompanied by bacteremia. Gastroenteritis typically occurs following the ingestion of contaminated water or food, while wound infections are usually the result of exposure to contaminated water. Although various virulence factors, such as endotoxins, hemolysins, enterotoxins, and adherence factors, have been identified in Aeromonas species, their exact roles in pathogenesis remain unclear. Aeromonas species are known to cause three main clinical conditions: 1) Opportunistic systemic infections in immunocompromised individuals. 2) Diarrheal disease in otherwise healthy individuals. 3) Wound infections. Gastroenteritis In children, gastrointestinal disease caused by Aeromonas is typically an acute and severe illness. In contrast, adults more commonly experience chronic diarrhea. Severe cases of Aeromonas gastroenteritis can mimic shigellosis, presenting with blood and leukocytes in the stool. Acute diarrheal disease caused by Aeromonas is generally self-limiting, and supportive care is sufficient for affected patients. Antimicrobial Therapy Antimicrobial treatment is necessary for patients with chronic diarrheal disease or systemic infections caused by Aeromonas. These bacteria are inherently resistant to penicillins, most cephalosporins, and erythromycin. While antimicrobial resistance is relatively uncommon in North America and Europe, resistant cases have been reported in Asia.
